sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The 23 July 1930, M 6.7 earthquake is one of the strongest events occurred in the Southern Apennines and also one that has been well documented, given the richness of the macroseismic information. Its intensity pattern somewhat resembles that of other historical major earthquakes for which a normal fault has been proposed in the literature as the causative source. A major difference, however, lies in the strike of the semi-axis of the macroseismic field, somehow in-betweens the circa NW-SE strike of the Apennines normal faults and that of the circa E-W strike-slip faulting proposed for the earthquakes that occurred in the foreland of the Southern Apennines.
Until recently, a number of focal mechanism had been proposed, based on various methods, and the results were quite different from one another. They ranged from almost pure normal faulting to oblique normal faulting, with the principal plane striking almost WNW-ESE. A recent re-evaluation of digitized seismograms by Pino et al. (2007) led to a new, more stable solution on which we based our interpretation.
This source shows a principal plane with the same strike as above and an oblique component, so that the source is characterised by normal kinematics with a right-lateral sense of motion. Also, the re-computed hypocenter, essentially in accordance with the coordinates previously proposed by Jimenez (1991), has been placed at about 14 km, i.e. slightly deeper than the hypocenter of the Irpinia 1980, M 6.8 event. For the latter event, in fact, a value of 12-13 km is a well accepted one - and one that provides a credible template for all major earthquakes caused by normal faulting in the Southern Apennines (Calabrian Arc excluded).
There is room to believe that the Irpinia 1930 event illustrated how the known stress field is exerted on faults with a strike somehow different from that of the major normal faults in the Southern Apennines. But we also believe that the Irpinia 1930 earthquake sheds some light on the mechanism of how earthquake faulting occurs farther to the east from the chain and, particularly, in an area which was repeatedly shaken by several strong earthquakes (including the 1930 one) in the last 3 centuries, namely the 8 Sep 1694 (M 6.9), 29 Nov 1732 (M 6.6), 14 Aug 1851 (M 6.3), and 7 June 1910 (M 5.9).
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Is such oblique slip at depth indicative of an interaction between the deeper E-W strike-slip, right-lateral reactivated shear zones and the comparatively shallower NW-SE trending normal faulting?
2) What is the structural relationship (if any) among the causative sources of the 1930, the 1732, the 1694, the 1851 and the 1910 earthquakes?
3) What are the roles (if any) of the buried Apulian platform and of the deep-seated basement on the occurrence and/or the development of deeply-rooted large seismogenic sources in this sector of the Southern Apennines?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Martini and Scarpa (1983)
These authors, among others, studied the 23 July 1930, Mw 6.7 earthquake. They present a focal mechanism showing normal faulting kinematics occurring along a circa E-W trending plane, with an oblique component. Also, they believe the hypocentral depth of this event to be located generically in the crust.
Jimenez (1991)
This author too studied the 23 July 1930, Mw 6.7 earthquake, using long-period 3-component, single station measurements. The author determined two possible focal mechanisms, depending on the velocity model adopted for southern Italy. Both solutions are based on a circa E-W trending plane; in both cases the conjugate plane trends N-S, but in one solution the dip of the conjugate plane is different, thus introducing an oblique component in the focal mechanism. The author estimates a hypocentral depth of approximately 14 km.
Emolo et al. (2004)
They examined the earthquake source of the 23 July 1930 event. Starting from the source models available in the literature, they simulated the acceleration field for each hypothesized model, and compared it with the macroseismic data. Then they employed a stochastic-deterministic technique to simulate ground motion associated with the rupture of a large fault. Finally, they associated the acceleration values simulated for several sites with the intensities using the empirical relationships, and then compared the former with the available macroseismic data. They conclude that a good reproduction of the macroseismic field is provided by a normal fault striking in Apenninic direction (approximately NW-SE) and dipping 55Â° toward the SW.
Pino et al. (2007)
These authors analysed historical waveforms from contemporary seismograms to study the geometry, kinematics and dynamics of the 1930 Irpinia buried fault. They identified the hypocenter at 14.6 km depth, while they recognised a N100Â°E striking rupture plane, dipping to the north and with an oblique motion. The fault they characterized is 32 km long; rupture propagated to the east.
